¶
'''weathering-stock†''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ing-stok), ''n.'' A post to which hawks are leashed in such a manner as to allow them limited exercise. See last quotation under ''weather'', ''v. t.'', 1.
{{smaller block|<poem>E’en like the hawk (whose keeper’s wary hands
Have made a pris’ner to her ''weath’ring stock'').</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, V. ix. 5.}}}}

'''weatherliness''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-li-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' Weatherly character or qualities: said of ships and boats.
{{smaller block|To combine the speed of the ordinary type of American sloop with the ''weatherliness'' of the English cutter.
{{right|''Science'', VI. 168.}}}}
'''2.''' ''Naut.'', the state of a vessel as to her capacity to ply speedily and quickly to windward.

'''weatherly''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-li), ''a.'' [< ''weather'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.] ''Naut.'', making very little leeway when close-hauled, even in a stiff breeze and heavy sea: noting a ship or boat.

¶
'''weather-strip''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-strip), ''n.'' A slender strip of some material intended to keep out wind and cold; originally, a strip of wood covered with soft material, as list or cloth; specifically, a contrivance by which a strip of india-rubber is adjusted closely to the apertures of a door or window, or its frame or jamb, covering the crevice very tightly: it is generally a wooden molding into which a thin strip of rubber is fitted.

'''weather-strip''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-strip), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''weather-stripped'', ppr. ''weather-stripping''. To apply weather-strips to; fit or secure with weather-strips.

'''weather-symbol''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-sim″bọl), ''n.'' A conventional sign used in meteorological records, or in published meteorological observations or weather-maps, to represent graphically any designated phenomenon. {{smaller|The following symbols have been adopted by the International Meteorological Congress to represent the principal hydrometeors and a few other phenomena. Rain, ●; snow, ✱; thunderstorm, ꓣ; lightning, ϟ; hail, ▲; mist, ≡; frost, ⫫; dew, ⍜; snowdrift, ⇸; high wind, ⥅; solar corona, ⊕; solar halo, ⦶; lunar corona, ⋓; lunar halo, ⩌; rainbow, ⌒; aurora, ᴥ; haze, dust haze, ∞.}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|weathered|6863|weather-symbol}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|{{right|''Darwin'', Geol. Observations, ii. 448.}}}}
{{smaller block|The force of the wind is such as actually to loosen the ''weathered'' parts of the rock and dislodge them.
{{right|''Geikie'', Geol. Sketches, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' Seasoned by exposure to the air or the weather.—'''3.''' In ''arch.'', having a slope or inclination to prevent the lodgment of water: noting surfaces approximately or theoretically horizontal, as those of window-sills, the tops of cornices, and the upper surface of flat stone-work.

'''weather-eye''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ī), ''n.'' The eye imagined to be specially used for the purpose of observing the sky in order to forecast the weather.—{{smaller|'''To keep one’s weather-eye open''' or '''awake,''' to be on one’s guard; have one’s wits about one. [Colloq.]}}
{{smaller block|Keep your ''weather eye awake'', and don’t make any more acquaintances, however handsome.
{{right|''Dickens'', Our Mutual Friend, ii. 5.}}}}

'''weather-fend''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-fend), ''v. t.''   [< ''weather'' + ''fend''<sup>1</sup>.]   To shelter; defend from the weather. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The line-grove which ''weather-fends'' your cell.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, v. 1. 10.}}}}

'''weather-fish''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-fish), ''n.'' The mud-fish, thunder-fish, or misgurn of Europe, ''Misgurnus fossilis:'' regarded as a weather-prophet because it is supposed to come out of the mud, in which it habitually burrows, before a storm.

'''weather-gage''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-gāj), ''n.'' '''1.''' ''Naut.'', the advantage of the wind; the position of a ship when she is to windward of another ship: opposed to ''lee-gage''.

{{smaller block|A ship is said to have the ''weather-gage'' of another when she is at the windward of her. {{right|''Admiral Smyth.''}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' Advantage of position; the upper hand.
{{smaller block|<poem>Were the line
Of Rokeby once combined with mine,
I gain the ''weather-gage'' of fate!</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, vi. 24.}}}}
'''To dispute the weather-gage.''' {{smaller|See ''dispute''.}}

'''weather-gall''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-gâl), ''n.'' Same as ''water-gall'', 2.

'''weather-glass''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-glȧs), ''n.''   [= D. ''weerglas'' = Sw. ''väderglas'' = Dan. ''veirglas'', barometer; as ''weather'' + ''glass''.]   An instrument designed to indicate the state of the atmosphere. {{smaller|This word is commonly applied to the barometer, but also to other instruments for measuring atmospheric changes and indicating the state of the weather, as the thermometer and various kinds of hygroscopes.}}
{{smaller block|The King of Spain’s health is the ''Weather-glass'' upon which all our politicians look; as that rises or falls, we look pleasant or uneasy. {{right|''Prior'' (Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 265).}}}}
'''Shepherd’s''' or '''poor man’s weather-glass.''' {{smaller|See ''shepherd''.}}

'''weather-gleam''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-glēm), ''n.'' A peculiar appearance of clear sky near the horizon. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|You have marked the lightning of the sky just above the horizon when clouds are about to break up and disappear. Whatever name you gave it, you would hardly improve on that of the ''weather-gleam'', which in some of our dialects it bears. {{right|''Trench.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}}

'''weather-hardened''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-här″dnd), ''a.'' Hardened by the weather; weather-beaten.
{{smaller block|A countenance which, ''weather-hardened'' as it was, might have given the painter a model for a Patriarch. {{right|''Southey'', The Doctor, ix.}}}}
'''weather-head''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-hed), ''n.'' '''1.''' A secondary rainbow.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''2.''' Stripes of cirrus cloud. [Scotch.]

'''weather-headed†''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-hed″ed), ''a.'' Same as ''wether-headed.''
{{smaller block|Sir, is this usage for your son?—for that old ''weather-headed'' fool, I know how to laugh at him; but you, Sir—.
{{right|''Congreve'', Love for Love, ii. 7. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''weather-house''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-hous), ''n.'' Same as ''weather-box.''   ''Cowper'', Task, i. 211.

'''weathering''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ing), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wederyng;'' verbal n. of ''weather'', ''v.'']   '''1†.''' Weather, especially favorable or fair weather.
{{smaller block|For alle trewe shipmen, and trewe pilgrymes, yat Godd for his grace yeue hem ''wederyng'' and passage, yat yei mowen sauely commen and gone.
{{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 23.}}}}
{{smaller block|Which would haue bene, with the ''weathering'' which we had, ten or twelve dayes worke.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', III. 515.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''geol.'', etc., the action of the elements in changing the color, texture, or composition of rock, in rounding off its edges, or gradually disintegrating it. {{smaller|The first effect of the weathering spar, and is the result of incipient decomposition and hydration. Rounding of the edges of angular projections of the rock, or of its constituents, is another result of weathering, the decomposed minerals being more easily removed by the action of water than they were before decomposition. Weathering is a preliminary to erosion, but the rapidity with which these operations are carried on varies greatly with the nature of the rock and the climatic and other conditions to which it is subjected.}}
{{smaller block|Many of them [nodules of various kinds] are, also, externally marked in the same direction with parallel ridges and furrows, which have not been produced by ''weathering.''
{{right|''Darwin'', Geol. Observations, i. 78.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''arch.'', a slight inclination given to an approximately horizontal surface to enable it to throw off water.

'''weathering-stock†''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ing-stok), ''n.'' A post to which hawks are leashed in such a manner as to allow them limited exercise. See last quotation under ''weather'', ''v. t.'', 1.
{{smaller block|<poem>E’en like the hawk (whose keeper’s wary hands
Have made a pris’ner to her ''weath’ring stock'').</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, V. ix. 5.}}}}

'''weatherliness''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-li-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' Weatherly character or qualities: said of ships and boats.
{{smaller block|To combine the speed of the ordinary type of American sloop with the ''weatherliness'' of the English cutter.
{{right|''Science'', VI. 168.}}}}
'''2.''' ''Naut.'', the state of a vessel as to her capacity to ply speedily and quickly to windward.

'''weatherly''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-li), ''a.''   [< ''weather'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   ''Naut.'', making very little leeway when close-hauled, even in a stiff breeze and heavy sea: noting a ship or boat.

{{smaller block|Notwithstanding her ''weatherly'' qualities, the heavy cross sea, as she drove into it, headed her off bodily.
{{right|''M. Scott'', Tom Cringle’s Log, {{sc|viii}}.}}}}

'''weather-map''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-map), ''n.'' A map showing the temperature, pressure, wind, weather, and other meteorological elements over an extensive region, compiled from simultaneous observations at a large number of stations. {{smaller|The pressure is represented by isobars, the temperature by isotherms, the wind by arrows, and the weather by differently shaded circles or other conventional symbols. Weather-maps, prepared once or twice daily, form the basis upon which every government weather-service forecasts the weather and issues storm-warnings.}}

'''weather-molding''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-mōl″ding), ''n.'' Same as ''dripstone'', 1.

'''weathermost''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-mōst), ''a. superl.''   [< ''weather'' + ''-most''.]   Furthest to windward.

'''weather-notation''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-nọ̄-tā″shọn), ''n.'' A system of abbreviation for the principal meteorological phenomena. {{smaller|Beaufort’s weather-notation, which is used in Great Britain, is as follows: ''b'', blue sky, whether clear or hazy; ''c'', clouds (detached); ''d'', drizzling rain; ''f'', fog; ''g'', very gloomy; ''h'', hail; ''l'', lightning; ''m'', mist; ''o'', overcast; ''p'', passing, temporary showers; ''q'', squally; ''r'', rain; ''s'', snow; ''t'', thunder; ''u'', ugly, threatening weather; ''w'', dew.}}

'''weather-plant''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-plant), ''n.'' The Indian licorice, ''Abrus precatorius'': so named in view of an alleged property of indicating the weather in advance. {{smaller|It is a common tropical twining shrub (see ''Abrus''), having pinnate leaves with from 20 to 40 small leaflets. Recent careful observations show that the pairs of leaflets fold together more or less as the light is stronger or weaker, the movement being less vigorous in a moister atmosphere; that a certain wrinkling of the surface coexists with a coloring of the margin likely to be due to the attacks of an insect; and that the movement of the rachis, supposed to be barometric, is a diurnal oscillation which varies in extent with the amount of light. The temperature also affects the freedom of those motions. These characteristics are all paralleled in other plants, especially of the ''Leguminosæ.'' As a means of forecasting, the plant is not likely to be of practical worth.}}

'''weather-proof''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-pröf), ''a.'' Proof against rough weather.
{{smaller block|<poem>Lord, thou hast given me a cell
Wherein to dwell,
A little house, whose humble roof
Is ''weather-proof.''</poem>
{{right|''Herrick'', A Thanksgiving to God for his House.}}}}
{{smaller block|There were only ten persons at the conference meeting last night, and seven of them were women; he wonders how many ''weather-proof'' Christians there are in the parish.
{{right|''C. D. Warner'', Backlog Studies, p. 72.}}}}

'''weather-prophet''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-prof″et), ''n.''   [=Dan. ''veir-profet''; as ''weather'' + ''prophet.'']   '''1.''' One who foretells weather; one skilled in foreseeing the changes or state of the weather. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Who that has read Greek does not know the humour with which the meteorological theories of the Athenian ''weather-prophets'' are ridiculed by Aristophanes in “The Clouds”?
{{right|''R. H. Scott'', in Modern Meteorology, p. 166.}}}}
{{smaller block|zation to the influence of atmospheric changes.
{{right|''Coues'', Birds of the Colorado Valley (1878), I. 372.}}}}

'''3.''' A device for foretelling changes in the weather. {{smaller|In most forms materials are employed which are so affected by dampness as to move some indicator, as a pair of figures, of which one appears or advances in dry and the other in wet weather. Other forms employ materials which change color according to the state of the atmosphere. Compare ''weather-box''.}}

'''weather-report''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-rē-pōrt″), ''n.'' A daily report of meteorological observations and of probable changes in the weather, especially one issued by a weather-service. [Colloq.]

'''weather-roll''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-rōl), ''n.'' The roll of a ship to windward, in a heavy sea on the beam: opposed to ''lee lurch''.

'''weather-service''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-sėr″vis), ''n.'' An institution organized for taking meteorological observations in accordance with a systematic plan, and for utilizing the data thus collected by forecasting the weather, issuing warnings of storms and floods, publishing climatological tables, distributing information as to the effect of the weather on growing crops, and by allied services. {{smaller|All the principal governments of the world now maintain a weather-service, upon which a part or all of these duties are imposed. In the United States an annual appropriation of nearly a million dollars is made to the Weather Bureau of the Department of Agriculture, which is charged with performing these services. In addition to the Weather Bureau, and coöperating with it, there is organized in nearly every State a State weather-service, composed of voluntary observers whose work is directed toward giving information upon the condition of the crops as affected by the weather, and in general toward extending knowledge of local climatology.}}

'''weather-shore''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-shōr), ''n.'' The shore from which the wind blows. {{smaller block|[The wind] set so violently as rais’d on the sudden so greate a sea that we could not recover the ''weather-shore'' for many houres.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Oct. 11, 1644.}}}}

'''weather-sign''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-sīn), ''n.'' Any phenomenon or sensation indicating state or change of weather; hence, generally, any prognostic or sign.
{{smaller block|<poem>I am not old for nothing; I can tell
The ''weather-signs'' of love; you love this man.</poem>
{{right|''Mrs. Browning'', Aurora Leigh, ii.}}}}

'''weather-spy''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-spī), ''n.'' One who foretells the weather; a weather-prophet.   ''Donne.'' [Rare.]

'''weather-stain''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-stān), ''n.''   [< ''weather'' + ''stain.'']   A stain or discoloration left or produced by the weather or by weathering.
{{smaller block|<poem>Walls must get the ''weather-stain''
Before they grow the ivy.</poem>
{{right|''Mrs. Browning'', Aurora Leigh, viii.}}}}
{{smaller block|He . . . felt that the shape and colour of every roof and ''weather-stain'' and broken hillock was good, because his growing senses had been fed on them.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, iii. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>With ''weather-stains'' upon the wall,
And stairways worn, and crazy doors.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Wayside Inn, Prelude.}}}}

'''weather-stained''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-stānd), ''a.'' Stained or discolored by the weather. See ''weathering'', 2.
{{smaller block|A tomb somewhat ''weather-stained.'' {{right|''Longfellow.''}}}}

'''weather-station''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-stā″shon), ''n.'' A station where daily meteorological observations are made and reported to a central office; one of the stations of a weather-service.

'''weather-strip''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-strip), ''n.'' A slender strip of some material intended to keep out wind and cold; originally, a strip of wood covered with soft material, as list or cloth; specifically, a contrivance by which a strip of india-rubber is adjusted closely to the apertures of a door or window, or its frame or jamb, covering the crevice very tightly: it is generally a wooden molding into which a thin strip of rubber is fitted.

'''weather-strip''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-strip), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''weather-stripped'', ppr. ''weather-stripping''. To apply weather-strips to; fit or secure with weather-strips.

'''weather-symbol''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-sim″bọl), ''n.'' A conventional sign used in meteorological records, or in published meteorological observations or weather-maps, to represent graphically any designated phenomenon. {{smaller|The following symbols have been adopted by the International Meteorological Congress to represent the principal hydrometeors and a few other phenomena. Rain, ●; snow, ✱; thunderstorm, ꓣ; lightning, ϟ; hail, ▲; mist, ≡; frost, ⫫; dew, ⍜; snowdrift, ⇸; high wind, ⥅; solar corona, ⊕; solar halo, ⦶; lunar corona, ⋓; lunar halo, ⩌; rainbow, ⌒; aurora, ᴥ; haze, dust haze, ∞.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
